newsitem.title: INDIA: India Hindu party eyes polls as coalition wrestles.
newsitem.headline: India Hindu party eyes polls as coalition wrestles.

text.p: India's opposition Hindu party has begun preparations for mid-term polls in case Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's ruling coalition unravels in the wake of last week's split in his own party.

How Gujral copes with the turmoil and reconciles pressures to banish his former party chief, Laloo Prasad Yadav, from the United Front alliance will be closely watched over the coming weeks, political leaders and analysts said.
The main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is rubbing its hands in anticipation of early elections as cracks surfaced in the ruling coalition, they said.
"We are in a win-win situation if there is an election," said BJP spokesman Yashwant Sinha.
Yadav, chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, quit Gujral's Janata Dal a week ago after failing to hold onto the party presidency in an election he says was rigged.

Yadav formed a splinter party called Rashtriya (Nationalist) Janata Dal, taking three ministers in Gujral's government with him. But he immediately pledged his support for the coalition and the ministers have retained their posts.
But Gujral's left-wing allies along with some key constituents of the United Front have asked him to ditch Yadav, who has been indicted in a $280 million corruption scandal.
"The left parties have been joined by other parties in the coalition in demanding that Laloo be kept out," Atul Anjan, a senior leader of Communist Party of India (CPI), told Reuters.
Yadav, a powerful low caste leader, says he is innocent and has rejected calls from coalition partners to step down as chief minister.
Gujral has adopted a passive strategy so far, for fear that any move could destabilise his fractious coalition, political analysts said.
"He has been unwilling to take a decision on Laloo and left it on the courts to decide," independent political analyst Rasheed Talib said.
But Yadav says he will face a confidence vote in the Bihar assembly during the monsoon session, which begins on Monday.
How the Congress party, which props up the UF coalition from outside to provide a secular bulwark against the Hindu nationalists, plays its hand in Bihar could determine Yadav's fate.

For now, analysts and political leaders reckon that, however rickety the coalition looks, Gujral will not lose his grip on power anytime soon, as an election would come too soon for the main opposition parties.
"The United Front government is safe," said Anjan.
But political analysts said the BJP was wooing regional parties in search of potential coalition allies.

The BJP, which emerged as the single largest party from inconclusive elections last year, feels it can improve upon its previous electoral performance if it can hammer a new alliance with some regional parties.
The Congress party was also waiting in the wings to grab a leading role in government.
Meanwhile, the political uncertainty has taken a toll on the functioning of the government as key economic decisions have been put on the hold, analysts said.
The decision making Steering Committee of the coalition has met twice unsuccessfully and deferred a decision on plugging the nation's rising oil subsidy bill.
"Vital issues of national concern remain unattended while the United Front tears itself apart on the issue of Laloo Prasad Yadav," BJP's Sinha said.
